newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS - Russia to buy more grain, Siberia harvest hit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Russia to buy more grain, Siberia harvest hit.

text.p: Russia on Tuesday revised upwards the amount of maize and soymeal it plans to buy this year from the West to four to 4.5 million tonnes and said downpours in Siberia could affect the total grain harvest.
Agriculture Minister Viktor Khlystun told an industry meeting in Russia's second city that Moscow would buy maize and soymeal from the United States, Canada and Australia this year.
"We intend to import 4.0-4.5 million tonnes of maize and soymeal, not only in 1996 but probably also in the coming years," he said.
Last month Khlystun said Russia would import three to four million tonnes of grains, mostly maize and soymeal, and about 500,000 tonnes of wheat this year.
Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Zaveryukha, who is in charge of the harvest, repeated earlier forecasts that the net harvest this year would be 75 to 77 million tonnes.
But he said a lot depended on Siberia.

"There are complex weather conditions in Siberia," Zaveryukha told the same industry meeting, adding that the Tomsk and Altai grain-growing regions had had steady rains for up to 10 weeks. "It (net output) will all depend on Siberia."
Other regions have experienced drought this summer but the effect will be milder than last year, when grain output dipped to 63.4 million tonnes, the worst in three decades.
Russia's grain imports will be mostly for the Far East, as well as for big cities and for reserves to feed the army.
Siberia is not Russia's main-grain growing area but its output is important because of the high cost of shipping grain from other regions to the far-flung Far East.
Traders have said imports from the United States, Canada and Australia could be more economical for Russia than shipping domestic grain from southern regions across the vast country.
Khlystun gave no details on when or how Russia would buy grain but said Russia needed maize, largely used here as a feed-grain. "Russia does not produce enough maize," he said.
Zaveryukha said Russia had harvested five million tonnes more grain than at this time last year but he gave no figures.
Other government and independent officials have put Russia's 1996 harvest in the range of 72-75 million tonnes.
